headline: Hormuz Standoff Clouds the Open as Inflation Data Looms
body_html:
Futures point to a cautious open Tuesday after Wall Street closed lower Monday as hopes for a swift resolution to the Strait of Hormuz impasse continued to dissolve. With Gulf shipping traffic through the waterway reported at just six vessels, crude prices have pushed markedly higher, amplifying anxiety across risk assets heading into the session. Gold extended its winning streak into a third consecutive day as investors sought shelter ahead of closely watched inflation prints due this week.

Monday's session was broadly negative in our coverage universe, with 321 names declining against 228 advancing out of 549 tracked. Semiconductors bore the sharpest sectoral damage, falling 3.11%, while Homebuilders shed 2.51% and Industrials dropped 1.30%. Energy was the lone sector to post meaningful gains, advancing 3.98% as offshore-services names surged in tandem with crude. Healthcare added 1.14%, providing a secondary pocket of relative strength.

At the open, traders will be watching for any diplomatic signals on the Hormuz corridor, which remains the dominant macro variable. The geopolitical backdrop — including the appointment of a known hardliner to Iran's top security body and fresh demands traded between Tehran and Washington — suggests no near-term de-escalation. Inflation data, when it arrives, will determine whether the rate outlook compounds or cushions the pressure on equities.

briefs.headline: Hormuz Shipping Collapses to a Trickle as Talks Stall
briefs.body: Gulf tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to just six vessels, according to reports, as US-Iran negotiations over conditions for reopening the critical waterway remain deadlocked. The drop in transit volume is already reverberating through energy markets, sending crude sharply higher and lifting offshore drilling and services equities on Monday.

briefs.headline: Energy Names Surge as Offshore Services Rally Leads the Tape
briefs.body: Valaris and Tidewater each climbed more than 8% in Monday's session, pacing gains in the Energy sector, which rose 3.98% — the only sector in positive territory on the day. The move reflects investor conviction that a prolonged Hormuz disruption will sustain elevated day-rates and demand for offshore drilling infrastructure globally.

briefs.headline: Iran Installs Hardline Figure Atop Key Security Council
briefs.body: Mohsen Rezaei, a figure known for an uncompromising posture toward the West, has been named secretary of Iran's supreme security body. The appointment is widely read as a signal that Tehran is in no hurry to soften its negotiating position on the Hormuz dispute, adding a fresh layer of geopolitical risk to an already unsettled energy market.

briefs.headline: N-able Suffers Steepest Single-Day Drop in the Universe
briefs.body: Managed-services software provider N-able saw its shares collapse 35.67% on Monday, the most severe decline across our entire 549-name coverage universe. No other name came close to that magnitude of selling, suggesting a company-specific catalyst — likely related to earnings or guidance — drove the outsized move.

briefs.headline: Gold Extends Rally as Safe-Haven Demand Builds Into CPI Week
briefs.body: Bullion rose for a third consecutive session Monday as investors positioned defensively ahead of this week's inflation releases. The combination of Hormuz-driven oil-price pressure and unresolved geopolitical tensions across multiple theatres is reinforcing appetite for the metal at a moment when rate-path uncertainty remains elevated.

briefs.headline: Semiconductor Stocks Take the Hardest Sectoral Hit
briefs.body: The semiconductor group fell 3.11% on Monday, the weakest sector performance of the session, as risk aversion and macro headwinds weighed on the group. MaxLinear led decliners within the space, tumbling 8.72%, while the broader chip cohort struggled against a backdrop of rising energy costs and fading appetite for high-beta growth names.
